overview: This entry begins in 1900, during the French protectorate, and continues through independence and the republic. Tunisia’s modern history includes political struggles as well as households making pottery and food, and communities adapting inherited settlements to changing needs.

periods.title: French protectorate
periods.summary: The protectorate, established in 1881, continued until independence on 20 March 1956.

periods.title: Independence and republican government
periods.summary: The monarchy gave way to a republic on 25 July 1957. The 2010 to 2011 revolution opened another political phase.

periods.title: Revolution and constitutional change
periods.summary: A constitution adopted in 2014 was followed by a new constitutional text in 2022.

sections.title: Political turning points and written words

items.text: The map’s 1900 label does not indicate an independent modern republic. France had imposed a protectorate in 1881. Independence came on 20 March 1956, initially with Lamine Bey as monarch; the republic was proclaimed in July 1957.

The 2014 constitution’s preamble commemorated the revolution of December 2010 to January 2011. Reading such a document tells us how its authors framed a political turning point; it does not mean every constitutional promise was fulfilled.

A written Arabic sample from article 4 is “حرية، كرامة، عدالة، نظام”: “Freedom, Dignity, Justice, Order”. This is the motto as printed in the historical 2014 constitution. Tunisia adopted a later constitution in 2022, so this sample is explicitly dated.

Women in Sejnane make terracotta cooking utensils, dolls and animal figures. UNESCO’s 2018 record follows the clay from wadi beds through cleaning, soaking, kneading and shaping: the finished object begins with knowing where useful earth can be found.

After firing, makers decorate the pots with two-tone geometric patterns associated with local tattooing and Amazigh weaving. The women also sell their work, while men participate in sales. It is a family economy with skilled women at its centre.

The Sejnane inventory gives a named example: potter Halima Saïdani taught her daughter Hajer, recorded as 17 and still at school. Craft learning and formal education could happen together, rather than belonging to separate worlds.

Sejnane makers adapt products to changing demand, and younger women can attend craft training. A tradition maintained by living people is capable of invention; it is not a pottery recipe frozen forever.

Harissa starts with chilli peppers dried in the sun, then split, stripped of stalks and seeds, washed and ground. Salt, garlic and coriander join the paste. A family preparation session can therefore involve a good deal of teamwork before anything reaches the table.

A mortar and pestle or a manual mincer can do the grinding, and the finished harissa is stored in glass or pottery. UNESCO describes women preparing it in convivial family or neighbourhood groups: kitchen work can also be social time.

On Djerba, a menzel combines a family estate with work and living space; groups of these form a houma neighbourhood. Farming and craft activities supported this dispersed settlement pattern, linked by roads to markets and places of worship.

Djerba’s older settlements included both dispersed Ibadi family estates and denser Jewish neighbourhoods. Massive houses and some fortified mosques also reflect insecurity and the need for refuge. The island’s architecture records cooperation and danger alike.

Modern tourism, transport and housing have changed Djerba. Some family estates retain their older uses while others have become second homes. UNESCO’s account treats the island as a changing community, not an untouched medieval exhibit.

ending.text: Tunisia continues. Independence and later constitutional changes transformed government, while communities retained and reworked their languages, crafts, food and built environments.
